problem: The consequence is stated backwards. If a student draws the inertia force and still writes ΣF = m a with all drawn arrows, the equation becomes (real net force) − m a = m a, so m a is counted twice and the reported acceleration comes out half the correct value, not double. With the worked-example numbers: 173.2 − 97.6 − 50a = 50a gives a = 0.756 m/s², which is half of 1.51 m/s².
fix: Writing ΣF = m a while the inertia force is also drawn on the diagram. That counts m a twice: the net real force is shared between two m a terms, so you report half the true acceleration. Choose one form and stay with it.

problem: Rounding slip. 50 × 1.51 = 75.5 N, not 75.6 N. The balance 173.2 = 97.6 + 75.6 only closes if a is carried as 1.512 m/s².
fix: Add an inertia force of 50 × 1.512 = 75.6 N backwards (about 75.5 N if you keep a = 1.51 m/s²); then 173.2 = 97.6 + 75.6, so the forces balance.

problem: The acceleration components are written as the English words at and an ("at changes the speed and an changes the direction"), which a student will read as the preposition and the article. The rest of the chapter uses <sub> tags.
fix: a<sub>t</sub> changes the speed and a<sub>n</sub> changes the direction.

problem: "taking ar and aθ from 5.2" is a bare section number: the symbols are not formatted and there is no link, so on a phone the reader cannot jump to the derivation of a<sub>r</sub> and a<sub>θ</sub>.
fix: taking ar and aθ from the chapter on cylindrical components.

problem: The section talks of brackets carrying an accelerating motor and of taking moments, which invites rigid-body use, but only the inertia force is mentioned. A body that also spins needs an inertia couple, so a student may apply the rule to a rotating bracket and drop that term. The chapter is written for particles, so the gap is easy to close.
fix: For the particle of this chapter the single inertia force is enough. A rigid body that spins as well also needs the inertia couple of magnitude I<sub>G</sub>α opposite to the angular acceleration, where I<sub>G</sub> is the mass moment of inertia about the centre of mass in kg·m² and α the angular acceleration in rad/s².
